meaning: Earth Mother; the land that gives birth to all living things

phonemes.desc: Voiceless bilabial plosive [p] plus open front [a]; Māori p is unaspirated and crisp.
Repeated syllable meaning 'earth, rock, foundation,' a reduplication common to Polynesian earth names.
Voiceless alveolar plosive [t] plus long close back rounded [uː]; tū means 'to stand.'
Long open central [aː], an emphatic particle in the compound.
Alveolar nasal [n] plus close back rounded [u], then voiceless velar stop [k] plus close back rounded [u]; nuku means 'extended, far-reaching.'

pronunciation.approximation: 'PAH-pah-too-AH-noo-koo' — keep the p's gentle and unaspirated, hold the ū and ā long, and give each vowel its own syllable.

pronunciation.note: The name is a transparent Māori compound. Papa means 'earth, rock, foundation' and is found across Polynesia; tū means 'to stand'; ā is an emphatic particle; nuku means 'extended, far-reaching.' The macrons on ū and ā mark long vowels, distinctive features the ASCII form loses, and they place the name in Tier 1. Some dialects and orthographies write the short form Papa.

domains.title: Earth Mother
domains.subtitle: Creation, Fertility, and the Land
domains.lead: Papatūānuku is the broad earth lying beneath the sky, the mother from whose body all living things spring. In Māori cosmology she and Ranginui, the Sky Father, were once locked in an embrace so tight that their children lived in darkness between them. Their separation by Tāne brought light and space into the world — and a wound of separation that still marks every creature's relation to earth and sky.

cards.name: Mother of Life
cards.desc: All plants, animals, and humans arise from her body; she is the source of nourishment and growth.

cards.name: Partner of Ranginui
cards.desc: The Sky Father lies upon her; their separation is the primal act of creation.

cards.name: Whenua and Identity
cards.desc: The land (whenua) is her body; Māori identity is inseparable from the earth that names and sustains the people.

cards.name: Return and Renewal
cards.desc: The dead return to her; she receives all things and makes them grow again.

symbols.name: Flat, dark earth
symbols.meaning: Her body is the soil itself, often figured as lying prone beneath the sky

symbols.name: Mountains and valleys
symbols.meaning: The folds and ridges of her body, the places where her children still touch her

symbols.name: Caves
symbols.meaning: Openings into her body, places of birth, burial, and communication with the dead

symbols.name: The kūmara and food plants
symbols.meaning: Crops grown from her body, especially the sweet potato brought from Hawaiki

mythology.lead: Papatūānuku's central myth — the separation of the Sky Father and Earth Mother — is the best-known creation narrative of Polynesia, recorded in many regional variants. The Māori versions written down in the nineteenth century by George Grey, Elsdon Best, and others differ in detail and genealogy, and all of them are transcripts of a living oral tradition rather than a fixed scripture. What the versions share is the argument: the world we inhabit is the aftermath of a family crisis, and its beauty and its grief are the same event seen from two sides.

myths.title: The Separation of Rangi and Papa
myths.text: In the beginning there was no sky above and no earth below in our sense — only Ranginui, the Sky, and Papatūānuku, the Earth, locked in an embrace so close that no light could enter. Their children were born into the narrow darkness between their parents' bodies: Tāne, Tāwhirimātea, Tangaroa, Tūmatauenga, Rongo, and Haumia-tiketike, with the unborn Rūaumoko stirring in the womb. Cramped and blind, the children debated their escape. Rongo-mā-Tāne and Tangaroa proposed killing the parents; Tāne counselled separation instead. Attempt after attempt failed — pushing from within, shoving from without — until Tāne lay on his back against his mother, braced his legs against his father, and thrust upward with the full strength of his body. Ranginui rose into the air with a great cry, light flooded the world, and the children stood for the first time in open space. (Grey, Polynesian Mythology; Best, Māori Religion and Mythology.) The myth insists that creation is not making something from nothing but the painful rearrangement of an original unity — space, light, and life all purchased at the price of the parents' grief.

myths.title: The Rain and the Mist
myths.text: Ranginui did not leave without mourning. From his eyes fell the rain, and Papatūānuku's longing rises from her body as the morning mist, so that the two remain in perpetual touch — his tears falling on her, her sighing rising to him. The versions differ on what happened next among the children: in Grey's telling, Tūmatauenga cursed his parents for what had been done and turned his anger on his brothers, while Tāwhirimātea fled to his father and never forgave the separation; only those who accepted their mother's gifts — the forests and birds to Tāne, the sea to Tangaroa, the kūmara to Rongo, the wild fernroot to Haumia — stayed close to her. The myth reads the weather as family feeling: every rainstorm is an embrace interrupted, and the mist at dawn is the earth answering the sky.

myths.title: Tāwhirimātea's War
myths.text: Tāwhirimātea, the wind, alone of the brothers refused to accept the separation. Furious at what Tāne had done to their parents, he fled to his father Ranginui, gathered an army of winds and clouds and squalls, and attacked his brothers one by one. He smashed Tāne's forests to splinters, broke Tangaroa's canoes and drove his grandchildren — the fish and the reptiles — into hiding in the sea's depths, and scattered the crops that Rongo had planted. Only Tūmatauenga stood against him and, though beaten, held his ground and did not flee. Defeated, Tāwhirimātea was driven back to the sky, where to this day he attacks Tangaroa, and his storms are the anger that never found peace. (Grey, Polynesian Mythology.) The myth gives weather a genealogy: storms are a brother's grief kept on the boil, and the calm between gales is the family's uneasy truce.

myths.title: The Earth's Welcome
myths.text: Papatūānuku is not only the beginning but the end. When people die, their bodies are returned to her — buried in her flesh, which is why Māori speak of the whenua, the land, and the whenua, the placenta, by the same word: both are the organ that feeds a person before they can feed themselves. From her body the dead pass onward, in many accounts, to the spirit world beyond, while her moisture rises as mist at dawn — sometimes remembered as her tears for Ranginui, sometimes as the milk with which she suckles her children still. The closing of the loop — birth from her body, life upon her body, return to her body — is the moral shape of the Māori cosmos, and it makes death not an exit from the world but a handover of one life back to its source.

lore.syncretism: Papatūānuku is cognate with the Hawaiian earth mother Papa and with earth-deity figures across eastern Polynesia; her partner Ranginui answers to the Rangi-sky figures of the whole triangle. In Māoridom today she is paired with Ranginui in prayers, environmental discourse, and artistic representations of the creation story. Some Christian Māori theologians have drawn parallels between Papatūānuku and the created earth praised in the biblical psalms, without identifying the two. Contemporary environmental movements invoke her as the personification of ecological responsibility: 'kaitiaki of Papatūānuku' — guardians of the earth — has become a standard formula of Māori land-rights and conservation rhetoric, giving an ancestral name to what the West calls sustainability.
lore.culturalLegacy: Papatūānuku has become a central figure in modern Māori cultural identity and in Aotearoa New Zealand's environmental and educational vocabulary. Schools, health services, and land-restoration projects invoke her name; environmental legislation and treaty settlements speak of the land in her terms. The phrase 'kaitiaki of Papatūānuku' expresses an ethic of guardianship that has entered national policy discourse. Internationally, she is one of the most widely recognized Polynesian deities, a symbol of indigenous earth-relationship in an era of climate crisis — proof that a nineteenth-century transcript of an older song can still govern how a nation thinks about its ground.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Papatūānuku is the earth not as resource but as ancestor. To stand on her is to stand on the body of a being who loved, who was separated from her partner, and who continues to give birth despite that grief. The Māori creation story does not begin with a single male creator speaking the world into order; it begins with an embrace so close that no one can breathe, and a separation that is also a wound.

In an age of ecological extraction, Papatūānuku offers a different grammar: the land is not something we have but someone we belong to. The name Papatūānuku, with its long vowels held like a breath, says that the earth is extended, standing, and reaching. We are her reach, her standing, her return.

lore.archaeology: There are no monumental temple sculptures of Papatūānuku comparable to those of Aztec or Greek deities; Māori sacred expression was primarily oral, architectural, and environmental. Marae and carved meeting houses (wharenui) encode genealogical narratives linking the living community to Papatūānuku and Ranginui — the meeting house itself is often read as the body of an ancestor, ridgepole as backbone, rafters as ribs. Rock art, greenstone ornaments, and burial practices reflect the cosmology of return to the earth. Nineteenth-century written records by Grey, Best, and Smith preserve the oral mythology in detail; the tradition they transcribed is itself the primary artifact.
